source.title: Harm Recognition to Refusal Gap: Why Small LLMs are unsafe?
source.citation: Harm Recognition to Refusal Gap: Why…

record.file_problem: None apparent; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes harmfulness and refusal as distinct representations and reports that their coupling relates to refusal outcomes, refining the single-direction account. It does not causally intervene on a refusal direction.
record.gate_note: The paper estimates harmfulness-related and refusal-related mean-difference directions, then measures their alignment and associations with refusal outcomes. It reports no ablation or addition of a direction. The CA-DPO results are deliberately trained behavior and evaluate the proposed training method, so they are not evidence that direction ablation or addition causes the claimed behavior.
record.test_reason: The study uses a different, correlational method on V5's question. It estimates a harmfulness direction (jailbreak minus clean, instruction position) and a refusal direction (refused minus non-refused, post-instruction) separately, then shows they are nearly orthogonal and that harm-loaded jailbreaks can still get compliance. It never ablates or adds a direction. Its 'refusal direction' is also not V1's harmful-minus-harmless direction, so V1 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that small models represent harmfulness, yet this signal does not reliably become refusal (a recognition-to-refusal gap), and that harm–refusal coupling tracks safety across scales better than refusal strength. They propose CA-DPO, which raises jailbreak refusal while keeping clean refusal, over-refusal and collapse low. All mechanistic evidence is correlational.
record.recipe_differences: Uses normalized mean-difference directions and activation projections, but examines separate harmfulness and refusal signals and their cosine relationship rather than ablating or adding a refusal direction.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported coupling varies across model sizes and layers; refused-versus-non-refused coupling comparisons are also reported separately by attack family.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 4: the jailbreak-derived harmfulness direction is shared across cipher, h4rm3l, and hand attack families (pairwise cos 0.556–0.587, LOFO separation about 1.85–1.93, Qwen3.5 0.8B–9B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The harmfulness direction is consistent across jailbreak attack families.

fits_no_version.finding: Fig. 3: the harm-to-refusal signal-strength ratio falls with model scale. Values 3.916, 2.194, 1.531 and 2.683 are shown for Qwen3.5-2B, Qwen3.5-27B, Llama3.2-11B and Llama3.2-1B; the mapping of values to bars is not readable from the text.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Coupling between harm recognition and refusal strengthens with model scale.

record.code_released: The paper says code and experiment scripts will be released in future work; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The coupling evidence is correlational and group-conditional, not a causal intervention. Table 1 reports no uncertainty estimates. The paper notes that its explanation may not generalize beyond the studied model families and configurations.
record.rows_left_out: CA-DPO benchmark and training-ablation results were not recorded as rows because the refusal behavior is deliberately induced by training and those results evaluate the proposed method, not the untrained direction mechanism.

untested.parts: All of it: no ablation, no addition, no capability check. The refusal direction is defined as refused minus non-refused, not harmful minus harmless.
Causal separation: no intervention on either direction to show one changes without the other.
No test that jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction, and no adversarial training against its ablation.
No affine, cone, or multi-direction comparison.
No cross-language, cross-variant, or base-to-instruct transfer.

missing.what: Over-refusal prompts give refusal-direction strength similar to jailbreaks despite a much weaker input-side harm signal. Refusal rates are also broadly comparable. This is refusal without a harm signal, bearing on V5.
Layer-wise harm–refusal cosine curves across Qwen3.5 0.8B–27B and Llama3.2 1B/11B.

record.verdict_notes: Changed tranche to T2 and removed V1 from every row. The study's refusal direction is an outcome contrast (refused minus non-refused jailbreaks), not Arditi's harmful-minus-harmless direction, and nothing is ablated or added. The reader's V1 labels are dropped. The CA-DPO results deliberately induce refusal through training and evaluate the authors' method, so they are correctly left out. Refusal is judged by keyword matching. Table 1 gives no uncertainty and covers only two models. Appendix A does not clearly explain how a refused-minus-non-refused contrast is estimated within a single outcome group.

versions.untested_parts: No projection or ablation at every layer and position; no addition or steering intervention; no test of whether general capabilities remain intact.
No test of whether jailbreaks suppress the direction, or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
The paper separates harmfulness and refusal directions but does not compare affine, cone, or multi-direction accounts of refusal.
The study measures distinct harmfulness-related and refusal-related representations, but does not causally isolate a harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
Directions are estimated separately for models; no cross-language, cross-variant direction transfer, or base-to-instruct transfer experiment.
No comparison of refusal-training histories or training stages for whether a single removable direction exists.

relation.reason: The study's own Table 1 cosines and its PCA and signal-strength analyses bear on whether harm recognition is encoded apart from refusal (V5).

tranche.reason: The study estimates harm and refusal directions as difference-in-means vectors, then compares their cosine and projections. It does no ablation or addition, so the method differs from the original, but it asks V5's question. It does not argue that any version is wrong or needs restating, so the reader's earlier T5 doesn't fit.

source_check.notes: The pack gives no [lN] id for the verdict, so l1 was assigned by position. The record's code=y is wrong: the text says code will be released later. Table 1's per-group method is unclear: it isn't explained how a refused-minus-non-refused direction is estimated inside one group. No random-direction baseline is given. Refused is above non-refused in all 6 pairs, but only by 0.010-0.056. Sec. 1 and Fig. 5 say coupling rises with model scale (figure-only), which may matter for V5 in larger models. The Fig. 7 caption says CA-DPO raises the refusal signal while the cosine stays low. The OpenReview footer addressed to reviewers is standard boilerplate for human reviewers, not instructions to an AI reader.

statements.correction: cDi2IoUNF2 (under review, ICLR 2027): code not released (the text says it will come in future work); no controls; no uncertainty. Table 1 has group-conditional harm vs refusal cosines for Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B, on cipher, h4rm3l and hand jailbreaks, refused and non-refused splits. All 12 values have |cos| <= 0.171 (max 0.171: 0.8B, hand, refused). No layer is stated. Correlational only, no intervention. Authors anonymous.
statements.problem: Two errors about this study. First, it says the study has code, but the reproducibility statement says code and scripts will be released in future work. Second, 'layers as stated' does not apply: Table 1 gives no layer. 'Four author groups' also can't be checked here, since this submission is double-blind and anonymous.
Makes no specific claim or number about this study. Its cross-study counts can't be checked from this text. 'Mostly correlational' fits this study, whose rows are all correlational.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: These are direction-level associations, not causal tests of a single direction; the study does not test the claimed ablation or addition effects (r3–r14).
